entries.name: Curtis Lab
entries.focus: The lab studies cancer as an evolving system, combining experimental, computational and AI/ML approaches. A central aim is to quantify and forecast tumour evolution, including very early evolution in precancer settings such as Barrett's esophagus and intestinal metaplasia. The lab also links genotype to phenotype in malignancy using multiomic profiling, single-cell and spatial transcriptomics, and organoid and computational models. A further goal is building reliable biomarkers to guide diagnosis, early detection and treatment decisions.

fit.reason: Strong overlap on cancer genomics, computational/ML methods and single-cell and spatial omics in cancer, with less emphasis on structural variants or bulk WGS/transcriptome pipelines; a US visa would likely be needed.

entries.name: Goodarzi Lab
entries.focus: The lab builds AI/ML models for in silico functional genomics. These include interpretable models of DNA and RNA regulation, plus large language and foundation models for chemistry and genomics. In cancer biology, it studies how tumour cells evolve and interact with their environment, with a focus on metastatic progression. Its work includes orphan non-coding RNAs (oncRNAs) that promote metastasis, and tRNA-derived fragments (tiRNAs) that suppress breast cancer metastasis. It also studies post-transcriptional regulatory programs in disease, and applies the same approach to neurodegenerative diseases.

fit.reason: The lab's ML for genomics and its cancer transcriptome and non-coding RNA work overlap with the student's interests. Its focus is metastasis and RNA regulation, not tumour WGS, structural variants or somatic mutation analysis, and a US visa would likely be needed.

entries.name: Van Loo Lab
entries.focus: The lab uses "molecular archeology of cancer" approaches to reconstruct how tumours evolve. It looks at evolutionary history, subclonal structure, metastatic spread and the emergence of therapy resistance. The work relies on computational analysis of large-scale cancer genomics data, including whole-genome sequencing, copy number and clonal evolution inference. It combines pan-cancer cohort studies with focused studies of individual tumour types.

fit.reason: Strong overlap with tumour WGS, somatic mutation and copy-number analysis, and computational methods for cancer genomics. Single-cell and spatial work is not evident from the pages I read, and a US visa may be needed.

entries.name: Alexandrov Lab
entries.focus: The lab studies the causes of cancer by analysing patterns of somatic mutation, known as mutational signatures, in tumour and normal-tissue genomes. A major strand is Mutographs, a consortium collecting about 5,000 cancer samples from more than 25 countries to identify the exposures behind these signatures. The lab also maintains the SigProfiler suite of machine-learning tools for next-generation sequencing data. Further work covers the mutational landscape of precancerous lesions (2,561 samples from 37 lesion types), duplex sequencing of normal tissues, and the Cancer Grand Challenges CAUSE project on DNA adducts.

fit.reason: Strong overlap with somatic mutation analysis, whole-genome cancer sequencing, structural/copy-number signatures and ML methods; little single-cell or spatial omics and no transcriptome focus, and the lab is in the US so a visa would be needed.

entries.name: Getz Lab
entries.focus: The lab studies cancer genomes through two linked steps. Characterization catalogues somatic and germline events and their causes by comparing tumour and normal samples. Interpretation analyses patient cohorts to find cancer-driving genes, pathways and molecular subtypes, and to relate them to clinical parameters and treatment outcomes. It builds computational tools and pipelines for large national and international cancer genome projects (for example TCGA and the Broad's genome and proteogenomics data analysis centres). These cover somatic mutation calling, resistance mechanisms and germline cancer risk.

fit.reason: Strong overlap with the student's cancer genomics, tumour WGS/somatic mutation analysis and computational methods interests, though I did not verify specific structural-variant or single-cell/spatial work. The US location may require a visa.

entries.name: Ideker Lab
entries.focus: The lab builds AI-driven, mechanistic models of cancer and neurodegenerative disease. The aim is to turn patient data into precision diagnosis and treatment. It maps genetic and molecular networks, such as the U2OS subcellular cell map and the Cancer Cell Map Initiative, and uses them to predict how genotype affects outcomes. It develops 'visible' (interpretable) machine learning for predictive oncology, including a recent foundation model that predicts therapeutic response from cancer genotype. Other work covers network biomarkers, the link between somatic mutation and epigenetic aging, and software such as Cytoscape, NDEx and iQuery.

fit.reason: The lab overlaps with the student's cancer genomics, somatic mutation and ML-for-genomics interests, but it centres on network and interpretable-ML models rather than WGS/transcriptome sequencing, structural variants or single-cell/spatial omics, and it would likely require a US visa.

entries.name: Laboratory of Evolutionary Design
entries.department_hint: Innovation Investigator, Arc Institute; Assistant Professor of Chemical Engineering, Stanford
entries.focus: The lab studies how evolution can be learned from data and then used for design. One theme is learning from nature: how the immune system balances short-term protection with long-term adaptability, with the aim of designing more robust therapeutics. A second theme is accelerating evolution by using machine learning to learn evolutionary rules from sequence data. A third theme is safe biological AI, meaning generative models that let researchers quickly counter harmful biology. Most of the work is machine learning on biological sequences.

entries.name: Palotie Lab
entries.focus: The group studies the genetic mechanisms of common diseases using clinical and population samples from the Finnish founder population. entries.focus: The lab studies how the tumour microenvironment changes as melanoma progresses from normal skin through precursor and in situ lesions to invasive disease. It also studies how a tumour cell's position relative to immune cells shapes its molecular state and drug response. Methods include multiplexed imaging (CyCIF), spatial transcriptomics, scRNA-seq, micro-region sequencing, and 3D tissue reconstruction. The computational side covers machine learning and statistics: the SCIMAP spatial single-cell Python toolkit, the GATOR deep-learning phenotyping framework, a spatial-lag algorithm, and an LDA-based model of recurrent cellular neighbourhoods.

entries.name: Martin Lab
entries.focus: The lab studies how human history shaped global genetic and phenotypic diversity. A main question is how well findings from Eurocentric genetic studies transfer to other ancestries. They develop and evaluate polygenic risk scores in multi-ancestry cohorts, including biobank and All of Us data, so that genetic prediction does not widen health disparities. They run psychiatric genetics case-control studies in African populations (for example NeuroGAP-Psychosis, with collaborators in eastern and southern Africa) and help train African researchers through the GINGER program. They also build community resources and statistical methods for diverse-ancestry data, such as the HGDP+1000 Genomes call set, and study fine-scale population structure and human evolution.

fit.reason: The lab does computational and statistical genomics, but on germline, population-level and polygenic work. It does not cover cancer genomics, tumour sequencing, somatic or structural variants, or single-cell and spatial omics, and a Canadian student would likely need a US visa.

entries.name: Klein Lab
entries.focus: The lab studies how cells make fate decisions during development, tissue homeostasis and regeneration. It looks for quantitative rules and predictive models of how fate choice and tissue organisation work. It builds time-resolved single-cell maps of differentiation in several model systems, including a comparative angle on immune cell evolution in the tunicate Ciona. The methods are droplet microfluidics single-cell RNA-seq (inDrop), CAGE core-shell capsules for multi-step and live-cell single-cell assays, lineage tracing, imaging reporters, and computational inference of lineage-resolved trajectories and feedback.

fit.reason: The overlap is in single-cell methods and computational/statistical genomics tools, but the lab works on developmental and stem-cell fate rather than cancer, tumour WGS, structural variants or somatic mutations, so the fit is only partial.

entries.name: Segre Lab
entries.focus: The lab develops statistical and computational methods to find the causal genes, variants and regulatory mechanisms behind common eye diseases. These include primary open-angle glaucoma, age-related macular degeneration (AMD) and diabetic retinopathy. Methods combine GWAS with functional genomics (eQTL and splicing QTL mapping in human retina), single-cell data and systems biology, with the aim of interpreting noncoding variants. Current directions include drug repurposing for glaucoma and AMD, pharmacogenomics of ocular drug response, and non-negative matrix factorization to find biological subtypes of glaucoma. The PI also did earlier GTEx work and developed the MAGENTA pathway-enrichment method for GWAS.

fit.reason: The computational methods and single-cell/functional genomics work overlap with the student's methods interests, but the lab studies germline genetics of eye diseases, not cancer, tumour WGS/transcriptomes or somatic structural variants, and a US role would likely need a visa.

entries.name: Burge Lab
entries.focus: The lab's tagline is 'Computational Biology of Gene Expression'. It studies how RNA-binding proteins (RBPs) recognise RNA. This includes preferences for RNA structure, bipartite motifs and local sequence context. The main assay is RNA Bind-n-Seq (RBNS), which measures affinity across millions of RNA sequences for dozens of RBPs. The lab also builds quantitative biophysical and probabilistic models of RBP-RNA binding and of splicing, including alternative splicing and spliceosome behaviour, and it studies how splicing couples to transcription and gene expression (for example intron-mediated enhancement). Broader themes are microRNA regulation, human variation and disease, and the evolution of gene regulation. The work combines computational and experimental approaches.

entries.name: Robinson Lab
entries.focus: The lab studies genetic influences on behavior and cognition. Robinson co-chairs the Psychiatric Genomics Consortium Autism Working Group and the Broad's NeuroDevelopmental Variability Initiative.

entries.name: Lahav Lab
entries.focus: The lab studies how single human cells turn signals into fate decisions such as growth, death, arrest and differentiation. They also ask why genetically identical cells respond differently. Most of the work is on the tumour suppressor p53, specifically how its dynamics after DNA damage determine cell fate, how p53 mutations change those dynamics, and how dynamics shape target-gene responses. Related projects cover DNA repair, cell growth and bHLH transcription-factor networks. Methods are live-cell fluorescence imaging of tagged proteins at single-cell resolution, quantitative image analysis, statistical analysis and mathematical modelling. The long-term goal is to use protein dynamics as a therapeutic target to steer healthy and cancer cells toward chosen outcomes.

entries.focus: The lab studies how evolution shapes and constrains the way organisms respond to their environment. It also asks how biochemistry, molecular design and pathway wiring let cells process environmental information, using duplicated genes within and across species to study quantitative features of pathways. entries.name: Talkowski Lab
entries.focus: The lab studies how genome structure relates to function and how genetic variation, especially structural variation, contributes to human disease. It builds methods and open resources for detecting and interpreting structural variants. These include population-scale SV maps and long-read efforts such as gnomAD-LR, and the lab also works on mobile element insertions and pangenome tools. It runs large-scale gene discovery and cellular modeling studies of autism and other neurodevelopmental disorders, including bipolar disorder. It also develops prenatal and pediatric genomic diagnostics. Work spans cloud-based computational pipelines, statistical and machine learning models, splicing and functional genomics, and high-throughput variant-to-function assays.

entries.name: Udler Lab
entries.focus: The lab works on precision diagnostics and management of diabetes. It analyses genetic data, from rare to common variants, to find new diabetes genes, disease subtypes and mechanisms. A major theme is defining molecular subtypes of type 2 diabetes with clustering of genetic loci and polygenic scores, so that patient care can be tailored. It also leads the RADIANT study of atypical diabetes, with patient recruitment at MGH and genomic analyses at the Broad. Data sources include UK Biobank, Mass General Brigham Biobank, All of Us and the T2D Knowledge Portal. The lab also runs the MGH Diabetes Genetics Clinic.

fit.reason: The lab is a computational human-genetics group focused on germline variation in diabetes. A US visa would also be needed.

entries.name: Hacohen Lab
entries.focus: The lab combines immunologists, geneticists, biochemists, technologists and computational biologists to study basic immune processes and immune-mediated diseases. Its methods include genome-wide genetic screens in primary immune cells, which led to the finding that STING is a proton channel. It also uses single-cell profiling to define cell types and disease-associated cell states in cancer immunity, sepsis and lupus nephritis, as part of the Human Cell Atlas. In cancer immunotherapy, it develops machine-learning methods to predict tumour neoantigens and has run personalized neoantigen vaccine trials in melanoma and glioblastoma. Current work includes deep learning in cancer immunology, same-cell multimodal methods for the tumour microenvironment, and neoantigen-targeting binder engineering.

fit.reason: There is solid overlap in single-cell/multimodal cancer omics and in machine learning for neoantigens and tumour immunity. The lab is immunology-centred, with little focus on whole-genome sequencing, structural variants or somatic mutation calling, and the student would need a US visa.

entries.name: Rigollet Lab
entries.focus: The group works on statistics, data science and AI, and currently concentrates on statistical optimal transport and the mathematical foundations of Transformers. Specific threads include Transformers viewed as interacting particle systems, where self-attention acts as a velocity field that clusters tokens. Another thread is Wasserstein gradient flows for particle-based optimisation over probability measures, used for variational inference and nonparametric maximum likelihood. On the biology side, they model cell populations as probability measures to predict treatment response and to reconstruct developmental trajectories. This work was funded by a Chan Zuckerberg Initiative single-cell grant, and the group collaborates with the Broad Institute.

It also builds scalable mixed-model association methods such as BOLT-LMM and heritability-estimation tools.

entries.name: Naqvi Lab
entries.focus: The lab studies the quantitative control of gene expression in development and the dosage 'tipping points' where small shifts in transcription factor levels cause rare and common disease, a framework it calls 'analog genomics'. It uses human pluripotent stem cell-derived models of development. It perturbs transcription factor function with chemical-genetic tools to titrate dosage. It combines this with functional genomics readouts such as multi-omic profiling and enhancer-usage mapping. Computational work includes sequence-to-activity deep learning and transfer learning to predict the sequence determinants of transcription factor dosage response, and the lab has published on dosage sensitivity in Nature Genetics (2023) and Cell Genomics (2025). The PI's earlier work covered the evolution of sex-biased gene expression in mammals and the genetics of human craniofacial and brain shape.

fit.reason: The lab shares the student's interest in computational and machine-learning methods for genomics, but it works on developmental gene regulation in stem cell models and has no cancer, tumour sequencing, structural variant or somatic mutation focus. It would also need a US visa.

entries.focus: The lab studies childhood brain tumors and leukemias, with a focus on pediatric brain tumors. It uses genome-wide DNA methylation profiling, analyzed with computational and machine learning methods, to classify tumor types, including rare ones. A methylation-based classifier developed by the lab is used in routine diagnostics. It also investigates non-mutational drivers, meaning epigenetic changes that switch on developmental genes in the wrong cellular context in tumors with few or no mutations in known cancer genes. Single-cell genomic techniques are used to study intratumor heterogeneity, subclonal evolution, cancer stem cell hierarchies, early tumorigenesis and therapy resistance.

fit.reason: Strong overlap with computational and ML methods for cancer genomics and with single-cell analysis of tumours, but the focus is pediatric brain tumour methylation and epigenetics rather than WGS, transcriptome or structural-variant analysis, and the role would need a US visa.

entries.name: Rothenberg Lab
entries.department_hint: Biology and Biological Engineering (gene regulatory network modelling; T-cell development)
entries.focus: The lab studies how multipotent blood progenitors commit to the T-cell lineage in the thymus. They treat this as a problem in gene regulatory network (GRN) logic. They examine how transcription factors such as Bcl11b, Lmo2, Hhex and others change in dosage and timing to control lineage choice and developmental pace. Current projects include age-related shifts in thymocyte potential toward innate lymphoid cells (ILCs) and innate-like γδ T cells. Another project uses quantitative proteomics to map protein-level regulation. Methods combine mouse and in vitro T-cell differentiation systems, genomic and epigenomic profiling, perturbation experiments, and computational GRN modelling.

fit.reason: The lab is strong in computational and genomic GRN analysis, but it studies normal T-cell development rather than cancer genomics, tumour WGS, structural variants or somatic mutations, so the overlap is limited to general genomics methods.

entries.name: Winfree Lab
entries.department_hint: Computer Science / Computation and Neural Systems / Bioengineering (molecular programming)
entries.focus: The group takes a synthetic approach to molecular programming. They build DNA- and RNA-based systems to find out what can be engineered with nucleic acids. Topics include algorithmic DNA self-assembly (tile assembly and DNA origami), in vitro biochemical circuits based on strand displacement, and chemical reaction networks. They also study DNA and RNA folding, fault-tolerant molecular computing, molecular self-replication, and the fundamental limits of computation in these systems. Current members also work on molecular motors, DNA condensates and liquid-liquid phase separation, and pattern formation in synthetic biology.

fit.reason: The lab does DNA nanotechnology and molecular computation, with no cancer genomics, sequencing, structural variant or single-cell/spatial omics work, so it overlaps almost nothing with the student's interests.

The approaches are evolutionary genomics, neurobiology and functional genetics.

entries.department_hint: Biology and Biological Engineering (Professor of Computational Biology; HMRI Investigator)
entries.focus: The lab works on three areas: cytoskeletal active matter, machine learning, and single-cell biology. The active matter work studies the mechanical self-organization of cellular structures. The machine learning work builds predictive models from high-dimensional data and uses them to reprogram and engineer biological systems. The single-cell work looks at cellular self-organization, for example in neural circuit development. Current members also work on LLMs and protein language models for single-cell genomics, predictive models of gene expression, and T-cell activation trajectories. One student works on tumour heterogeneity and cell-cell communication.

entries.name: Guttman Lab
entries.department_hint: Biology and Biological Engineering (experimental plus computational genomics)
entries.focus: The lab studies how non-coding RNAs shape nuclear structure and gene expression. A major model is the lncRNA Xist and X-chromosome inactivation. The lab also studies nuclear compartments such as nuclear speckles and their link to splicing efficiency, and RNA-mediated neurodegeneration (the C9ORF72 repeat expansion in ALS). It builds its own multiplexed genomics tools, including SPRITE (3D genome contacts among DNA, RNA and protein), CLAP and SPIDR (RNA-protein interaction mapping) and ChIP-DIP (protein-DNA mapping). It combines these experimental methods with computational analysis, and its newer work includes single-cell functional genomics and CRISPRi screens.

fit.reason: The lab combines genomics method development with computation and some single-cell work, but it focuses on basic RNA and nuclear biology, with no cancer, tumour sequencing, structural variant or somatic mutation work. A US visa may also be needed.

entries.focus: The lab develops principles, mechanisms and algorithms for the rational design of dynamic molecular devices made from nucleic acids, working in vitro, in situ and in vivo. A third theme is single-cell genomics, covering clonal evolution, the timing of somatic mutations and their fitness effects. The group also analyses somatic mutations in sequencing data, and the PI received an ERC Consolidator Grant in December 2025 on genome structure and gene regulation in disease.

fit.reason: Very strong overlap with the student's interests in cancer WGS, structural variants and somatic mutation analysis, computational methods, and single-cell cancer genomics, but the lab is UK-based, so a visa would likely be needed.

It also has smaller cancer-genomics projects, including tumour progression modelling co-advised with the Van Allen lab.

entries.focus: The lab studies how proteins bind each other in eukaryotic signaling, and how binding specificity arises. It combines computational modeling, including structure-based and machine-learning models, with experiments such as yeast surface display and photo-crosslinking. One long-running focus is the Bcl-2 family and its BH3-motif helices. The lab has used this work to design peptide reagents that profile apoptotic status in cancer cells. The lab also studies short linear motif-binding domains (TRAF, EVH1, E3 ligase Itch) and designs selective peptide binders and inhibitors of protein–protein interfaces.

fit.reason: The lab is a computational and experimental protein-design group with only a tangential link to cancer (apoptosis profiling). It does no genomics, sequencing, structural-variant or single-cell work, so overlap with the student's ML-for-genomics interest is limited.

entries.name: Page Lab
entries.focus: The Page lab studies how males and females differ genetically, both in and outside the reproductive tract, and how those differences affect biology and medicine. Its work spans comparative, evolutionary, developmental and clinical analyses. It sequenced the sex chromosomes of eight mammals and chickens. That work found Y-linked genes that are active throughout the body and regulate chromatin, transcription, translation and protein stability. Current questions include how sex chromosome makeup (X and Y dosage) shapes sex differences in gene expression and sex biases in disease. The lab also develops methods for highly accurate sequencing of complex, repetitive genomic regions. It uses mouse models to study germ cell development, which bears on infertility and germ cell cancers.

fit.reason: The lab has strong computational genomics and sequencing methods, and it touches germ cell cancers, but its main focus is sex-chromosome biology and not tumour WGS, structural variants, somatic mutations or single-cell/spatial cancer omics. A US visa would also likely be needed.

Related work covers epigenetic memory through mitosis and cell fate, and the nuclear mechanics and organization of chromatin. Methods are mainly polymer simulations, Hi-C and other chromosome-conformation data analysis, Bayesian inference and some machine learning. The lab has also done cancer-evolution work, including past students who went on to cancer genomics, but this is not its main current focus.

fit.reason: The lab is computational and uses Hi-C and some single-cell data, but it is focused on chromatin biophysics rather than cancer genomics, tumour sequencing, structural variants or somatic mutations, so overlap is limited to general computational-methods skills.

Its aim is to enable reliable microbiome-based therapies. A central approach is to infer within-person bacterial evolution from whole-genome sequencing of cultured isolates, using new computational methods. Co-existing lineages in a host preserve a record of their history, so this works without longitudinal sampling. The lab also uses high-throughput culturing, develops computational tools, and studies the spatial structure of microbiomes, with a focus on the human environment.

fit.reason: The lab shares the student's interest in computational methods for whole-genome sequencing and in mutation calling, but it works on bacterial microbiome evolution, not cancer genomics, structural variants, or single-cell/spatial cancer omics.

entries.name: Greener Group (biomolecular simulation / force fields)
entries.focus: The group works to make molecular dynamics simulations more accurate for biology. Current force fields can fail on disordered proteins and protein aggregation. One approach trains faster molecular mechanics force fields with graph neural networks, using quantum mechanics and experimental data. The aim is a reproducible method that works across all biomolecules. A second approach builds fast machine learning interatomic potentials for biomolecular systems, using simpler models and GPU programming, with the long-term goal of simulating enzyme reactions. The group also works on differentiable simulation (the Molly.jl package in Julia), protein design with simulation, protein folding and free-energy methods.

fit.reason: The group does ML-driven biomolecular simulation and force-field development, with no cancer genomics, sequencing, structural variant or single-cell/spatial omics work, so it overlaps with the student only through general computational and ML methods.

entries.focus: The lab studies functional genetic variation in human populations. entries.focus: The lab develops computational methods for structure-based drug discovery and applies them to therapeutically relevant targets. It builds the next-generation AutoDock suite (AutoDock-GPU, Vina-based tools), with GPU-accelerated docking engines and improved energy scoring. Members also run virtual screening on membrane proteins and combine docking with AI-driven molecular modeling, often jointly with experimental labs at Scripps.

entries.name: Alsentzer Lab
entries.focus: The lab applies machine learning and natural language processing to support clinical decision-making and expand access to high-quality healthcare. One theme is integrating domain knowledge, such as biomedical knowledge graphs and unstructured clinical text, into models for generalizable decision support. Recent work includes evaluating LLMs on real-world clinical text, monitoring deployed AI systems, and assessing AI-generated discharge summaries. Student projects also cover rare-disease diagnosis and reasoning over longitudinal clinical records alongside patient molecular data.

entries.name: Lundberg Lab
entries.focus: The lab works at the intersection of bioimaging, spatial proteomics and AI. Its goal is to define the spatiotemporal organization of the human proteome at the cellular and subcellular level. It maintains the Subcellular Atlas of the Human Protein Atlas (HPA), together with a Stockholm group. Methods include immunofluorescence microscopy, multiplexed imaging, mass-spectrometry proteomics and Deep Visual Proteomics. On the computational side, members build deep learning, self-supervised, diffusion and foundation models of protein localization and cell state, aiming at integrated models and 'digital twins' of human cells. Disease applications include primary cilia, cell migration and metastasis markers, and early cancer risk factors.

fit.reason: The lab's strengths are ML and spatial protein imaging, which loosely overlap with the student's interest in computational methods and spatial omics. It does essentially no cancer genomics, WGS/transcriptome sequencing or structural variant work, and the role would be in the US and need a visa.

entries.name: Salzman Lab
entries.focus: The lab treats genomic data as a statistical signal-processing problem, with an emphasis on splicing, cancer and microbes. A flagship method is SPLASH (and the related NOMAD), a reference-free, alignment-agnostic statistical framework. It finds sequence variation directly from raw reads, including alternative splicing, gene fusions, RNA editing, and diversity-generating elements in microbes. Other work covers circular RNAs, new statistics for spatial and single-cell sequencing data (for example MERFISH), and gene-fusion discovery in cancer. The lab also uses deep learning to predict phenotypes and antibiotic or drug response.

entries.name: Steinmetz Lab

Methods include single-cell multi-omics, multiplexed CRISPR and precision genome editing, and CRISPR screens. Cancer is not a stated focus.

entries.name: Rivas Lab
entries.focus: The lab uses large-scale genomic and phenotypic data, mainly from population biobanks, to study human genetics with computational and statistical methods. Recent work includes ultra-rare variant meta-regression of exome sequencing data from about 21,000 epilepsy cases and 33,000 controls. It also includes polygenic prediction with the univariate guided lasso in biobanks, and LLM-informed priors for re-analysing exome results in schizophrenia, autism, epilepsy, IBD and obesity. Current members work on AI tools for tumour boards, quantum computing algorithms for genetics, and clinical-trial optimization. The focus is germline and population genetics rather than tumour sequencing.

fit.reason: There is overlap in computational and ML methods for genomics, and two members work on AI tumour-board tools, but the lab centres on germline and biobank genetics, with no evident focus on tumour WGS, structural variants, somatic mutation or single-cell and spatial omics.

entries.name: Stanford Center for Biomedical Informatics Research (BMIR)
entries.focus: The lab works on semantic technology, ontologies and knowledge representation for biomedicine. Its projects include Protégé (ontology development), the National Center for Biomedical Ontology/BioPortal, and CEDAR (the Center for Expanded Data Annotation and Retrieval, for authoring metadata for experimental datasets). The work is about making biomedical data findable and reusable through standardized metadata. It is not about generating or analysing omics data.

fit.reason: The lab works on ontologies and metadata infrastructure, so it has almost no overlap with cancer genomics, structural variants or single-cell/spatial omics. The only link is that metadata standards could support genomics data sharing.

entries.name: Covert Lab
entries.focus: The lab builds computational models of complex biological systems and uses them to guide experiments, which speeds up the discovery of unknown components and interactions. It is known for whole-cell models, which simulate every gene and molecular process of a single organism such as E. coli or Mycoplasma genitalium. It also does live-cell microscopy and single-cell imaging of signalling dynamics. A current focus is NF-kappaB, a transcription factor family whose abnormal activity is linked to cancer development, tumour progression and chemotherapy resistance. Work on metabolic, regulatory and signalling networks and on cell-cell interactions uses mathematical modelling together with experiments.

fit.reason: The lab's computational and single-cell methods and its NF-kappaB cancer-signalling angle overlap only loosely with the student's interests; it does not work on tumour sequencing, structural variants, somatic mutations or cancer genomics, and a US role may need a visa.

entries.name: Snyder Lab
entries.focus: The lab develops and applies high-throughput 'omics' (genomics, transcriptomics, proteomics, metabolomics, epigenomics and microbiome profiling). Its main application is longitudinal personal multi-omics profiling for precision health, including wearable-sensor data and the integrative personal omics profile. Current work includes multi-omics and machine learning for disease risk and progression, aging, the exposome, immune responses to infection and vaccination, the gut microbiome, and cardiovascular and metabolic disease. The lab also does some cancer work (immunotherapy, drug resistance and epigenomics in organoids, and perturbation biology), but it is a small part of the lab's output. Computational method development is substantial, for example metabolomics algorithms, mass-spectrometry tools and multi-omic integration.

fit.reason: Strong on computational and machine-learning genomics and multi-omics integration, but the lab is mostly precision health and wearables, with only a few cancer-focused members (e.g. Shubham Gupta, Shannon White, Jou-Ho Shih) and little on tumour WGS, structural variants or single-cell/spatial work.

entries.name: Rusu Lab
entries.focus: The lab develops analytic methods for integrating biomedical data, especially multimodal fusion. A core approach is radiology-pathology fusion, which uses registration to map histopathology labels onto MRI so that radiology images can be labeled for training. Another is MRI-ultrasound fusion to guide procedures. These feed multimodal deep learning models for detecting cancer and predicting its extent and subtype, mainly in prostate, breast and kidney cancer. Work includes computer vision, self-supervised learning and robust medical AI. It is imaging-centred, not sequencing-centred.

fit.reason: The lab does machine learning for cancer, which loosely overlaps with the student's computational methods interest. It works on radiology and histopathology imaging, not genomics, structural variants, sequencing or single-cell/spatial omics, and it is in the US, so a visa may be needed.

entries.name: Gevaert Lab
entries.focus: The lab develops machine learning methods for biomedical decision support, centred on 'biomedical data fusion'. This means integrating molecular (omics), cellular (pathology) and tissue-level (medical imaging) data. Its listed research areas are multi-omics data fusion, quantitative imaging (radiogenomics), computational pathology, computational epigenomics, and network modelling for drug discovery. Earlier work included Bayesian and kernel methods for breast and ovarian cancer, and algorithms that identify driver genes from multi-omics data. Current members work on deep learning for histology and genomics in brain cancer, digital pathology, and imaging-based prediction.

fit.reason: Strong overlap in cancer ML and multi-omics integration, but the lab emphasises imaging and pathology rather than WGS, structural variants or single-cell/spatial omics, and a US role would likely need a visa.

fit.reason: The lab does structural biology and drug discovery with MD and ML, with essentially no overlap with cancer genomics, tumour sequencing, structural variants, or single-cell/spatial omics. The only common ground is general ML methods development, and a US position would likely need a visa.

entries.name: Altman Lab
entries.focus: The lab applies AI, data science and informatics to medicine, especially drug action and drug response at the molecular, cellular, organism and population levels. It maintains PharmGKB, a pharmacogenomics knowledge base linking genotype to drug response. It analyzes 3D protein structures to find binding and active sites for small-molecule drugs and runs physics-based simulations of biological structures. Cancer genomics, structural variants and single-cell or spatial omics are not named as core themes on the pages I read.

fit.reason: There is some overlap in ML and computational genomics methods, but the lab's core is pharmacogenomics, protein structure and biomedical NLP rather than cancer WGS/transcriptome, structural variants or single-cell/spatial omics, and a US role would likely need a visa.

entries.focus: The lab works on systems genomics for population health, with a focus on cardiovascular and cardiometabolic disease. The work is population-scale and statistical, not tumour sequencing.

entries.name: Erban Group (mathematical and computational methods for biological systems)
entries.focus: The group develops mathematical and computational methods for biological systems, centred on multiscale and stochastic modelling. Topics include stochastic simulation of chemical reaction networks and reaction-diffusion processes. The group also works on bifurcation and dynamics analysis of stochastic gene regulatory networks, and on collective behaviour of interacting particles and cells. Methods are mainly applied mathematics: stochastic differential equations, PDEs, and coarse-graining or multiscale algorithms. The group also writes software for reaction-diffusion modelling. Applications include tissue growth and apoptosis, and aggregate-level tumour-growth modelling. It does not work on sequencing data.

fit.reason: The group does theoretical and applied-mathematics modelling of stochastic biochemical and cellular systems. It has essentially no overlap with cancer genomics, sequencing, structural variants, or single-cell and spatial omics, and only a loose link through machine learning or computational methods.

This includes PRDM9 and hotspot biology, models of how DNA sequence shapes recombination, and single-cell meiosis data. The other main theme is fine-scale population structure within countries, and the genetic effects of migration in humans and other species. The group builds methods and software, including genotype imputation and phasing with reference panels and genome-wide genealogy inference (Relate). It also works on GWAS in stratified cohorts and the genetics of extreme phenotypes. Its work is germline and population-genetic. It does not cover tumour or somatic genomics.

entries.focus: The lab studies how cell type programs and their genome regulation evolve. It uses comparative regulatory genomics across animals and unicellular eukaryotes. entries.focus: The group combines large-scale DNA mutagenesis experiments (deep mutational scanning), genomics, biophysics, mechanistic modelling and AI to learn how sequence changes alter proteins and RNAs. Its work covers how the immune system develops, how it is maintained, and its role in infection, inflammation and disease. A major thread is human skin: immune cells in skin and skin organoids, prenatal skin development, and therapeutic response in atopic dermatitis. The group contributes to the Human Cell Atlas, and members work on multimodal data, single-cell lineage tracing and population cohorts such as JAGUAR. The group's published focus is immunology, development and inflammatory disease rather than cancer.

fit.reason: The group does strong single-cell and computational genomics, which overlaps with the student's methods interests, but the focus is immunology, development and inflammatory disease rather than cancer genomics, structural variants or somatic mutation, and the UK role would likely need a visa.

flags: No move: Haniffa remains at the Wellcome Sanger Institute and holds a joint Newcastle University professorship.

entries.name: Soranzo Group
entries.focus: The group studies the genetic basis of complex human traits with population-scale genomic analyses. Its data include SNP-array and whole-genome sequencing studies of quantitative risk factors and inflammation/immunity biomarkers. entries.name: Bayraktar Group
entries.focus: The group explores human brain cellular diversity using large-scale approaches. It combines spatial transcriptomics, high-throughput imaging and functional screening to study neural cell types in health and disease. It has three research directions: large-scale spatial transcriptomics of human tissues, cortical cell type diversity in health and disease, and large-scale glial function screens. The group also builds computational tools for spatial data, including cell2location for mapping cell types.

entries.name: Meta FAIR
entries.focus: FAIR Chemistry builds open datasets and machine-learning models for molecules and materials. It grew out of the Open Catalyst Project. Its OMol25 dataset, built with Berkeley Lab, has over 100 million DFT-calculated 3D molecular snapshots of up to 350 atoms. It covers most of the periodic table, with biomolecules, electrolytes and metal complexes as the three main focus areas. Alongside it, FAIR released the Universal Model for Atoms (UMA), an equivariant graph neural network. UMA is trained on more than 500M DFT calculations and is meant to work out of the box as an atomistic simulation model. The work is molecular and atomistic (chemistry, catalysis, materials, biomolecular interactions). I found no genomics, sequencing or cancer-biology programme on this team.
